lessons.title: Measuring prolactin and finding the cause
lessons.objective: Know whom to test for prolactin under each guideline, draw and repeat the sample properly, exclude non-tumour causes, recognise macroprolactin and the hook effect, and decide when to order MRI.
lessons.closing: Prolactin with clinical features (NICE, ESHRE, ASRM) or also for infertility (pituitary consensus statements). Mild rise: repeat at rest. Pregnancy, drugs, TSH, kidney and liver before MRI. No symptoms: macroprolactin; large tumour with a low value: dilution.

lessons.title: Treatment with dopamine agonists
lessons.objective: Choose the agonist and dose according to the sources, know whom not to treat, monitor adverse effects and valves, plan withdrawal and manage antipsychotic-induced hyperprolactinaemia with psychiatry.
lessons.closing: Cabergoline first (bromocriptine where it is unavailable). Microadenoma without symptoms or wish to conceive: observe or hormone replacement. Echocardiography by the 2 mg/week threshold. Withdrawal after > 2 years on a low dose with tumour shrinkage. Antipsychotics: with psychiatry, suspect tumour > 10 times the limit.

lessons.title: Fertility, pregnancy and breastfeeding
lessons.objective: Prepare for pregnancy in a woman with prolactinoma, know when to stop the agonist, how to monitor micro- and macroadenomas during pregnancy and what the sources say about breastfeeding.
lessons.closing: Macroadenoma: response (or surgery) before conception. On confirming pregnancy, stop the agonist. Microadenoma: clinical check every 3 months; macroadenoma: monthly and visual fields quarterly. Symptoms: MRI without gadolinium and restart the agonist. Breastfeeding is usually allowed.

items.title: Who should have prolactin measured? Guidelines disagree
items.core: NICE NG257 advises against measuring prolactin in people concerned about their fertility and offers it only with an ovulatory disorder, galactorrhoea or a pituitary tumour. [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]] ESHRE 2023 does not recommend prolactin testing in unexplained infertility (strong; very low certainty, ⊕), and the ESHRE 2022 recurrent pregnancy loss guideline does not either, unless there are symptoms of hyperprolactinaemia such as oligo/amenorrhoea (conditional). [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]] [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]
items.body:
ASRM 2021 also leaves prolactin out of the routine infertility evaluation and indicates it with galactorrhoea, oligomenorrhoea or amenorrhoea. [[ref:asrm-2021-fertility-evaluation]] By contrast, the 2023 Pituitary Society consensus states that loss of libido and/or infertility, new-onset menstrual irregularity or amenorrhoea should trigger investigation for hyperprolactinaemia (strong), as should galactorrhoea outside pregnancy and lactation (strong). [[ref:petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus]] The 2025 Chinese consensus recommends measuring it in women of reproductive age with menstrual disorders, infertility and/or galactorrhoea (low certainty; strong). [[ref:cpasc-2026-prolactinoma-consensus]]

In short: NICE, ESHRE and ASRM restrict the test to women with clinical features (disturbed cycles or galactorrhoea); the pituitary consensus statements count infertility itself as sufficient reason. [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]] [[ref:petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus]]
items.recall: Which guidelines order prolactin for infertility alone, and which only with an ovulatory disorder or galactorrhoea?
items.pearl: With regular cycles and no galactorrhoea, fertility guidelines do not order prolactin: the result is unlikely to change anything, and a borderline value opens an unnecessary work-up.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: NICE NG257 1.18.11 [2004] (p. 27). ESHRE UI 2023 rec. 34, strong, ⊕ (p. 71). ESHRE RPL 2022, prolactin conditional (p. 11). ASRM 2021 (pp. 4 and 7). Pituitary Society 2023 (pp. 723–724): galactorrhoea and infertility/menstrual disturbance, strong. 2025 Chinese consensus, recommendation 1: low certainty; strong. In the 2023 Pituitary Society consensus, “strong” rests on moderate- or high-quality evidence and “weak” on low- or very-low-quality evidence (Box 1, p. 724). In the 2025 Chinese consensus, GRADE certainty runs from very low to high and strength is strong or weak; GPS = good practice statement.

items.title: How to draw the sample and when to repeat it
items.core: According to the 2023 Pituitary Society consensus, venipuncture stress can raise prolactin two- to fourfold for less than 1 hour; values < 5 times the upper limit of normal should be repeated, and cannulated sampling is recommended if stress is suspected (strong). [[ref:petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus]] The 2025 Chinese consensus advises sampling at rest, after an overnight fast and at least 2 hours after waking, and repeating if prolactin is < 100 ng/ml (2120 mU/L). [[ref:cpasc-2026-prolactinoma-consensus]]
items.body:
The Pituitary Society adds that exercise, high-protein meals and alcohol can raise prolactin physiologically, and that stimulation and suppression tests give non-specific results and have largely been abandoned. [[ref:petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus]] The Chinese consensus describes pulsatile secretion, higher during sleep and early morning, with a nadir between 10:00 and 12:00. [[ref:cpasc-2026-prolactinoma-consensus]]

Watch the units: 1 μg/L equals 21.2 mIU/L, normal values are higher in women than in men, and published upper limits are lower than those of many manufacturers, so the assay’s own intervals should be used. [[ref:petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus]]
items.recall: How much can venipuncture stress raise prolactin, and when should the sample be repeated under each consensus?
items.pearl: A mildly raised prolactin after a difficult draw, early in the morning or after training is not a diagnosis: it is a reason to repeat the sample properly.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: Pituitary Society 2023, “Causes of hyperprolactinaemia” (p. 724): repeat with < 5 × ULN and cannula if stress, strong; text and “Prolactin assays” (pp. 724–725). 2025 Chinese consensus, recommendation 1 text (sampling conditions and repeat if < 100 ng/ml; not a separately graded recommendation). In the 2023 Pituitary Society consensus, “strong” rests on moderate- or high-quality evidence and “weak” on low- or very-low-quality evidence (Box 1, p. 724).

items.title: Before thinking prolactinoma: pregnancy, drugs, thyroid, kidney and liver
items.core: The 2023 Pituitary Society consensus recommends rigorously reviewing medication to exclude drug-induced hyperprolactinaemia, recognising primary hypothyroidism, renal insufficiency and liver failure as causes of mild elevations, and not overlooking pregnancy (all strong). [[ref:petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus]] The 2025 Chinese consensus requires excluding physiological, pharmacological and other pathological causes before diagnosing a prolactinoma, starting by ruling out pregnancy and reviewing drugs (GPS). [[ref:cpasc-2026-prolactinoma-consensus]]
items.body:
Among physiological causes, the Pituitary Society lists pregnancy, breast or nipple stimulation, stress, sleep, coitus and exercise; among drugs, neuroleptics and antipsychotics (for example risperidone and haloperidol), metoclopramide, domperidone, methyldopa, verapamil, opiates, tricyclic antidepressants and SSRIs; oral contraceptives are listed as a controversial cause. [[ref:petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus]] The hyperprolactinaemia of primary hypothyroidism reverses with thyroid hormone; lesions compressing the pituitary stalk raise prolactin by removing the dopaminergic brake. [[ref:petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus]]

In PCOS, raised prolactin needs further evaluation, because PCOS itself is rarely associated with hyperprolactinaemia. [[ref:petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus]] Neither this consensus nor the Chinese one mentions herbal remedies (such as chasteberry or vitex) or supplements to lower prolactin: these sources make no recommendation on them. [[ref:petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus]] [[ref:cpasc-2026-prolactinoma-consensus]]
items.recall: Which non-tumour causes of hyperprolactinaemia must be excluded before diagnosing a prolactinoma?
items.pearl: Pregnancy test, TSH and a full drug list (including antiemetics and psychotropics) before ordering an MRI.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: Pituitary Society 2023, “Causes of hyperprolactinaemia” (p. 724), strong; Box 2 (p. 726). 2025 Chinese consensus, recommendation 4: GPS. The absence of any herbal recommendation refers only to these two sources. In the 2023 Pituitary Society consensus, “strong” rests on moderate- or high-quality evidence and “weak” on low- or very-low-quality evidence (Box 1, p. 724). In the 2025 Chinese consensus, GRADE certainty runs from very low to high and strength is strong or weak; GPS = good practice statement.

items.title: Macroprolactin and the hook effect: two laboratory traps
items.core: The 2023 Pituitary Society consensus recommends testing for macroprolactin when prolactin is moderately raised (< 200 ng/ml), at least when clinical or imaging findings are discordant (strong), and diluting the sample 1:100 for a giant adenoma with clinical hyperprolactinaemia and normal or mildly raised prolactin, to exclude the hook effect (strong). [[ref:petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus]] The 2025 Chinese consensus makes the same proposals with less strength: macroprolactin when clinical findings are discordant and dilution for macroadenomas with normal or mildly raised prolactin (low certainty; weak). [[ref:cpasc-2026-prolactinoma-consensus]]
items.body:
Macroprolactin (prolactin–IgG complexes) is found in 10–25% of hyperprolactinaemia cases according to the Pituitary Society and is biologically inactive, so most of these patients have no symptoms; polyethylene glycol precipitation usually distinguishes it. [[ref:petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus]] The Chinese consensus gives a frequency of 5.32–22.90% and considers a monomeric prolactin recovery < 40% after PEG suggestive of macroprolactinaemia. [[ref:cpasc-2026-prolactinoma-consensus]]

The hook effect is rare with current assays; the Chinese consensus suggests suspecting it especially with tumours of maximum diameter ≥ 3 cm and prolactin < 100 ng/ml. [[ref:cpasc-2026-prolactinoma-consensus]] With inconsistent symptoms and values, the Pituitary Society also asks to consider biotin or heterophile antibodies (strong). [[ref:petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus]]
items.recall: When should you order macroprolactin and when a 1:100 dilution, and how strongly does each consensus recommend it?
items.pearl: High prolactin without symptoms: think macroprolactin. Large tumour with prolactin “only slightly high”: ask for dilution.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: Pituitary Society 2023, “Biochemical evaluation” (p. 725), strong; text (pp. 725–726). 2025 Chinese consensus, recommendations 2 and 3: low certainty; weak. Neither source gives an explicit recommendation on treating isolated macroprolactinaemia; they only describe it as inactive. In the 2023 Pituitary Society consensus, “strong” rests on moderate- or high-quality evidence and “weak” on low- or very-low-quality evidence (Box 1, p. 724). In the 2025 Chinese consensus, GRADE certainty runs from very low to high and strength is strong or weak; GPS = good practice statement.

items.title: Pituitary MRI: when, and how to read the result
items.core: The 2023 Pituitary Society consensus recommends MRI once hyperprolactinaemia is confirmed if no other non-adenomatous cause is evident (strong). [[ref:petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus]] The 2025 Chinese consensus indicates it after excluding physiological, pharmacological and systemic causes (low certainty; weak) and proposes dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI to detect microadenomas better (very low; weak). [[ref:cpasc-2026-prolactinoma-consensus]]
items.body:
In its diagnostic algorithm, the Pituitary Society notes that with moderate elevations (≤ 200 ng/ml) diagnoses other than prolactinoma should be considered; with an adenoma and moderately raised prolactin, a stalk effect from a non-functioning adenoma. [[ref:petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus]] Adenoma size and prolactin usually correlate, and discordance should prompt consideration of other causes (strong). [[ref:petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus]]

Imaging follow-up is individualised; the Pituitary Society asks for repeat MRI with treatment resistance, new symptoms (vision, headache, galactorrhoea), new pituitary dysfunction or rising prolactin (strong), and considers serial imaging beyond the first year unnecessary for responding tumours if prolactin does not rise. [[ref:petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus]] The Chinese consensus notes gadolinium retention and prefers macrocyclic agents. [[ref:cpasc-2026-prolactinoma-consensus]]
items.recall: When should you order pituitary MRI, and what does prolactin ≤ 200 ng/ml with a large adenoma suggest?
items.pearl: A macroadenoma with a prolactin of 60 is not a “poorly responding macroprolactinoma”: it may be a non-functioning adenoma with stalk effect, or a hook effect.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: Pituitary Society 2023, “Imaging” (p. 726), strong; Fig. 2 (p. 727); size–prolactin discordance (p. 724), strong. 2025 Chinese consensus, recommendations 6 (low; weak and very low; weak) and 7 (GPS). In the 2023 Pituitary Society consensus, “strong” rests on moderate- or high-quality evidence and “weak” on low- or very-low-quality evidence (Box 1, p. 724). In the 2025 Chinese consensus, GRADE certainty runs from very low to high and strength is strong or weak; GPS = good practice statement.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman (fictional case) with regular 28-day cycles and no galactorrhoea attends after 18 months trying to conceive; the basic work-up is normal (unexplained infertility). What do NICE NG257 and ESHRE 2023 say about prolactin?

options.text: Measure it in every woman with infertility
options.why: That is the broader stance of the pituitary consensus statements, not that of NICE or ESHRE.

options.text: Do not measure it: only with an ovulatory disorder, galactorrhoea or pituitary tumour (NICE); not recommended in unexplained infertility (ESHRE)
options.why: Correct: NICE 1.18.11 and ESHRE rec. 34 (strong; very low certainty, ⊕).

options.text: Measure it only in the mid-luteal phase
options.why: Neither guideline sets a cycle phase for prolactin.
The Pituitary Society notes that stimulation tests give non-specific results and have largely been abandoned.

items.explanation: Fertility guidelines restrict prolactin to women with clinical features; the Pituitary Society and the Chinese consensus include infertility as a reason to measure it. It is a real disagreement worth knowing.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman (fictional case) with oligomenorrhoea has a prolactin of 1.8 times the upper limit, drawn after three failed attempts. TSH is normal and the pregnancy test is negative. What is most appropriate per the 2023 Pituitary Society consensus?

options.why: Hyperprolactinaemia must be confirmed first: with < 5 times the limit the measurement is repeated.
MRI is ordered once hyperprolactinaemia is confirmed and no other cause is evident.

options.text: Repeat prolactin, with a cannula if stress is suspected
options.why: Correct: repeat with < 5 × ULN and cannulated sampling if stress is suspected (both strong).

options.text: Disregard the result and not measure it again
options.why: There is oligomenorrhoea, a reason to investigate hyperprolactinaemia; the value should be repeated, not ignored.

items.explanation: Venipuncture stress can raise prolactin two- to fourfold for less than 1 hour; a mild rise is confirmed before looking for an adenoma.

items.stem: At a check-up, a 38-year-old woman (fictional case) with regular cycles, no galactorrhoea and no headache has a prolactin of 90 ng/ml, confirmed on a second resting sample. She takes no drugs; her pregnancy test is negative and TSH, renal and liver function are normal. What is the most reasonable next step?

options.why: Correct: moderate elevation with discordant clinical findings; the Pituitary Society recommends it (strong) and so does the Chinese consensus (weak).
Without confirming that the prolactin is biologically active and without symptoms, there is nothing to treat yet.
Dilution is reserved for large adenomas with normal or mildly raised prolactin.
Stimulation and suppression tests give non-specific results.

items.explanation: Macroprolactin is common (10–25% per the Pituitary Society) and biologically inactive: it explains high values without symptoms and avoids unnecessary MRI and treatment.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man (fictional case) has a 4 cm pituitary macroadenoma with hypogonadism and a prolactin of 55 ng/ml. What should you ask for before labelling it non-functioning?

options.why: Macroprolactin explains high values without symptoms, not low values with a large tumour.

options.text: Repeat prolactin on a 1:100 diluted sample
options.why: Correct: it excludes the hook effect (Pituitary Society, strong; Chinese consensus, weak, especially with tumours ≥ 3 cm).

options.text: Cannulated prolactin after 30 minutes of rest
options.why: It helps exclude stress as the cause of a mild rise, not a falsely low value.

options.text: Nothing: at 55 ng/ml prolactinoma is excluded
options.why: With extremely high concentrations, the assay can return only a moderately raised value.

items.explanation: In two-site assays, a vast excess of prolactin saturates the antibodies and gives a falsely low value; diluting the sample reveals the true value and changes treatment (agonist instead of surgery).

items.title: Cabergoline versus bromocriptine
items.core: The 2023 Pituitary Society consensus considers cabergoline the preferred dopamine agonist because of its long half-life, efficacy and tolerability (strong); bromocriptine and quinagolide are used less, depending on regional approval and availability. [[ref:petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus]] NICE NG257 (2026) offers cabergoline for ovulatory disorders due to hyperprolactinaemia, instead of the bromocriptine it recommended in 2013. [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.body:
Usual doses per the Pituitary Society: cabergoline 0.5–3.5 mg per week (the maximum FDA-approved dose is 2 mg weekly), bromocriptine 2.5–15 mg per day and quinagolide 75–300 μg per day. [[ref:petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus]] NICE justifies the switch by fewer adverse effects, lower cost and once-weekly dosing. [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]

The 2025 Chinese consensus gives the same ranges (bromocriptine in 2–3 doses; cabergoline half-life 80 h) and suggests starting cabergoline at 0.25–0.5 mg/week or bromocriptine at 0.625–1.25 mg/day; in one trial, bromocriptine caused more nausea (≈ 50% versus 31%) and more discontinuation for adverse effects (12% versus 3%). [[ref:cpasc-2026-prolactinoma-consensus]] Because cabergoline is unavailable in mainland China, bromocriptine remains the first choice there. [[ref:cpasc-2026-prolactinoma-consensus]]
items.recall: Why is cabergoline preferred, and what dose ranges do the consensus statements give for cabergoline and bromocriptine?
items.pearl: Availability changes the recommendation: check which agonists are marketed in your country before following a foreign guideline to the letter.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: Pituitary Society 2023, “Dopamine agonists: efficacy” (p. 729), strong; doses in the text (p. 729). NICE NG257 1.32.1 [2026] (p. 38) and rationale (p. 75). 2025 Chinese consensus, recommendation 9 text (moderate; strong). Availability of each drug in Argentina or Spain has not been verified (AEMPS/CIMA and ANMAT not consulted). In the 2023 Pituitary Society consensus, “strong” rests on moderate- or high-quality evidence and “weak” on low- or very-low-quality evidence (Box 1, p. 724). In the 2025 Chinese consensus, GRADE certainty runs from very low to high and strength is strong or weak; GPS = good practice statement.

items.title: Not every hyperprolactinaemia needs an agonist
items.core: For the 2023 Pituitary Society consensus, women with hyperprolactinaemia or microprolactinoma and normal gonadal function can be observed (weak), and in premenopausal women with microprolactinoma not seeking pregnancy one option is hormone replacement without other interventions (strong). [[ref:petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus]] The 2025 Chinese consensus suggests observing microprolactinoma without clinical hyperprolactinaemia and treating if symptoms appear or it grows (very low; weak). [[ref:cpasc-2026-prolactinoma-consensus]]
items.body:
Combined contraceptives can be used with an agonist, but they may reduce its efficacy and sustain galactorrhoea (weak); when starting an agonist in someone not seeking pregnancy, barrier contraception is advised because pregnancy can occur before menses return (weak). [[ref:petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus]] After menopause, a microprolactinoma may need no intervention and can be followed with annual prolactin (weak). [[ref:petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus]]

On surgery, the two consensus statements agree more than they differ: for microprolactinomas and well-circumscribed macroprolactinomas (Knosp 0–1), both present it as a first-line option alongside an agonist. The Pituitary Society asks for surgery by an expert pituitary neurosurgeon to be discussed with the patient before medical treatment starts (strong), while using cabergoline as primary medical therapy; the Chinese consensus lets the patient choose between surgery and an agonist according to preference (low; weak). [[ref:petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus]] [[ref:cpasc-2026-prolactinoma-consensus]]
items.recall: What options does a woman with microprolactinoma not seeking pregnancy have, and where do the consensus statements disagree on surgery?
items.pearl: Without a wish for pregnancy, the aim in microprolactinoma is oestrogen status and symptoms, not “normalising the number”.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: Pituitary Society 2023, “Hypogonadism” (p. 728) and “Dopamine agonists: efficacy” (p. 729); surgery (p. 731), strong. 2025 Chinese consensus, recommendations 10 (low; weak) and 12 (very low; weak). In the 2023 Pituitary Society consensus, “strong” rests on moderate- or high-quality evidence and “weak” on low- or very-low-quality evidence (Box 1, p. 724). In the 2025 Chinese consensus, GRADE certainty runs from very low to high and strength is strong or weak; GPS = good practice statement.

items.title: Adverse effects: early nausea, impulsivity to watch
items.core: The 2023 Pituitary Society consensus asks clinicians to warn, before starting, about the frequent mild adverse effects of cabergoline (gastrointestinal, dizziness, fatigue) (strong); taking it at bedtime or with food and starting low may improve tolerability (weak). [[ref:petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus]] Agonists can cause neuropsychiatric effects such as compulsive buying, gambling, aggression, mood changes or hypersexuality; if they appear, the drug should be stopped or the dose adjusted (strong). [[ref:petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus]]
items.body:
Impulsivity is more frequent in men but occurs in both sexes and is not dose-related; the Pituitary Society suggests also asking the partner and family, because the patient may hide behaviours such as gambling. [[ref:petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus]] The 2025 Chinese consensus cites a highly variable incidence of impulse control disorders (9.8–52%) and asks for information and monitoring especially in men, people under 40 and those with a history of smoking, alcohol, anxiety or depression. [[ref:cpasc-2026-prolactinoma-consensus]]

If cabergoline intolerance persists, the Pituitary Society suggests trying another D2 agonist such as quinagolide (weak). [[ref:petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus]]
items.recall: Which cabergoline adverse effects should be explained at the start, and what should be done about an impulse control disorder?
items.pearl: Ask at every visit about spending, gambling and behaviour change: patients rarely volunteer it.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: Pituitary Society 2023, “Dopamine agonists: adverse effects” (p. 729), strong/weak per bullet; text (pp. 729–731). 2025 Chinese consensus, recommendation 9 text. In the 2023 Pituitary Society consensus, “strong” rests on moderate- or high-quality evidence and “weak” on low- or very-low-quality evidence (Box 1, p. 724).

items.title: Cabergoline and heart valves: when to order echocardiography
items.core: The 2023 Pituitary Society consensus proposes baseline echocardiography if long-term cabergoline > 2.0 mg per week is anticipated, repeated every 2–3 years at those doses; with ≤ 2.0 mg per week, echocardiography after 5–6 years; and with a murmur, echocardiography (all weak). [[ref:petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus]] The 2025 Chinese consensus recommends periodic echocardiography with long-term high-dose cabergoline (low certainty; weak). [[ref:cpasc-2026-prolactinoma-consensus]]
items.body:
Some Pituitary Society participants considered repeat studies unnecessary with < 1.0 mg per week and no signs of valve disease, and most considered annual cardiac examination unnecessary; the consensus acknowledges that intervals vary between countries and that it departs somewhat from earlier recommendations. [[ref:petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus]]

The Chinese consensus cites an incidence of cabergoline-associated valvulopathy of 0.11% in prolactinoma, advises in its text a baseline echocardiogram before starting treatment, indicates echocardiography with doses > 2 mg/week, more than 5 years of treatment, age > 50 or a murmur, proposes repeating it every 2–3 years and does not support routine echocardiographic monitoring with bromocriptine. [[ref:cpasc-2026-prolactinoma-consensus]]
items.recall: When should echocardiography be ordered for a patient on 1 mg of cabergoline weekly, and when on 3 mg weekly?
items.pearl: The dose threshold shared by both consensus statements is 2 mg per week; the Chinese consensus adds more than 5 years of treatment or age > 50, and in both a murmur brings the study forward.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: Pituitary Society 2023, “Dopamine agonists: cardiac valvulopathy” (p. 731), weak; based on the joint guidance of the British Society of Echocardiography, the British Heart Valve Society and the Society for Endocrinology. 2025 Chinese consensus, recommendation 14 (low; weak). In the 2023 Pituitary Society consensus, “strong” rests on moderate- or high-quality evidence and “weak” on low- or very-low-quality evidence (Box 1, p. 724). In the 2025 Chinese consensus, GRADE certainty runs from very low to high and strength is strong or weak; GPS = good practice statement.

items.title: Stopping the agonist: who, and how to follow up
items.core: According to the 2023 Pituitary Society consensus, about one in five patients remains in remission after stopping cabergoline, so dose reduction or withdrawal should be assessed periodically (strong); success is predicted by a low maintenance dose, more than 2 years of treatment and substantial adenoma shrinkage (strong). [[ref:petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus]] The 2025 Chinese consensus proposes considering withdrawal after more than 2 years on a low maintenance dose, with normal prolactin and notable tumour shrinkage or no visible mass on MRI (very low; weak). [[ref:cpasc-2026-prolactinoma-consensus]]
items.body:
The best chance is with a small non-invasive adenoma, normal prolactin and tumour shrinkage after at least 2 years of low-dose cabergoline (0.25–0.50 mg per week): in that subgroup, about 55% of micro- and 43% of macroprolactinomas stay in remission. [[ref:petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus]] After withdrawal, prolactin every 3 months in the first year and then annually (or sooner if symptoms recur), lifelong; if it relapses, the agonist usually works again (strong), and menopause or a pregnancy increases the chance of resolution (weak). [[ref:petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus]]

The Chinese consensus cites a meta-analysis with remission after withdrawal of 21% in micro- and 16% in macroadenomas, 34% if treatment lasted more than 2 years, and 35% with cabergoline versus 20% with bromocriptine. [[ref:cpasc-2026-prolactinoma-consensus]]
items.recall: Which three predictors of successful withdrawal do the consensus statements cite, and how is prolactin followed afterwards?
items.pearl: After a pregnancy or at menopause is a good time to try withdrawal.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: Pituitary Society 2023, “Dopamine agonists: treatment withdrawal” (p. 731), strong/weak per bullet; text (p. 731). 2025 Chinese consensus, recommendations 15–18 (low or very low; weak). In the 2023 Pituitary Society consensus, “strong” rests on moderate- or high-quality evidence and “weak” on low- or very-low-quality evidence (Box 1, p. 724). In the 2025 Chinese consensus, GRADE certainty runs from very low to high and strength is strong or weak; GPS = good practice statement.

items.title: Antipsychotic-induced hyperprolactinaemia
items.core: The 2023 Pituitary Society consensus recommends measuring prolactin before starting an antipsychotic (strong) and suspecting a prolactinoma if it exceeds 10 times the upper limit, because that is uncommon in antipsychotic-induced hyperprolactinaemia (strong). [[ref:petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus]] Reducing the dose or switching to a second-generation antipsychotic that does not raise prolactin, such as aripiprazole, distinguishes prolactinoma from the drug cause in most patients (strong); MRI may exclude a large lesion with stalk effect (weak). [[ref:petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus]]
items.body:
Hyperprolactinaemia occurs in 30–75% of people receiving antipsychotics within the first 3 months, and it resolves within 48–96 hours of withdrawal. [[ref:petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus]] MRI is indicated with prolactin > 10 times the limit, mass symptoms (headache, visual disturbance) or pituitary deficits other than gonadal. [[ref:petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus]]

Managing a prolactinoma with psychiatric illness requires collaboration with psychiatry (strong); starting an agonist is probably safe but needs caution and psychiatric input (weak), its efficacy may be lower (weak), and adding aripiprazole may allow dose reduction (weak). [[ref:petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus]]
items.recall: Which prolactin threshold raises suspicion of prolactinoma in someone on antipsychotics, and which strategy helps tell them apart?
items.pearl: With amenorrhoea and galactorrhoea on risperidone, coordinate with the psychiatrist before changing the antipsychotic or prescribing cabergoline; MRI does not wait if prolactin exceeds 10 times the upper limit or there are mass symptoms or other pituitary deficits.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: Pituitary Society 2023, “Patients with an underlying psychiatric disorder” (p. 736), strong/weak per bullet; text (p. 736). The 2025 Chinese consensus has no specific antipsychotic recommendations. In the 2023 Pituitary Society consensus, “strong” rests on moderate- or high-quality evidence and “weak” on low- or very-low-quality evidence (Box 1, p. 724).

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman (fictional case) with amenorrhoea, a wish to conceive and a confirmed microprolactinoma chooses medical treatment. Which agonist do NICE NG257 and the 2023 Pituitary Society consensus offer?

options.why: NICE recommended it in 2013; in 2026 it replaced it with cabergoline. It remains first choice where cabergoline is unavailable, as in mainland China.
Correct: NICE 1.32.1 [2026] and the Pituitary Society (strong) for efficacy, tolerability and weekly dosing.
It is not a treatment for hyperprolactinaemia in these sources.
They would prevent pregnancy; they may also reduce agonist efficacy.

items.explanation: NICE justifies cabergoline by fewer adverse effects, lower cost and weekly dosing; the Pituitary Society, by its long half-life, efficacy and tolerability.

items.stem: A 36-year-old woman (fictional case) has taken cabergoline 1 mg per week for 1 year, with no murmur. Per the 2023 Pituitary Society consensus, when is echocardiography due?

options.why: Most of the panel considered annual cardiac examination unnecessary.
That interval is for doses > 2.0 mg per week.
Correct: with ≤ 2.0 mg per week, echocardiography after 5–6 years (weak); some consider it unnecessary below 1.0 mg without signs.

options.text: Never; prolactinoma doses carry no risk
options.why: The consensus asks clinicians to inform patients of the rare risk of valve changes with long-term and/or high-dose treatment (strong).

items.explanation: The practical threshold is 2 mg per week: above it, baseline and every 2–3 years; below it, after 5–6 years. A murmur brings the study forward.

items.stem: Which of these patients (fictional cases) is the best candidate for a cabergoline withdrawal trial?

options.text: Microprolactinoma, 8 months of treatment, 2 mg per week
options.why: She lacks treatment duration (> 2 years) and a low maintenance dose.

options.text: Microprolactinoma, 3 years on 0.25 mg per week, normal prolactin and no visible mass on MRI
options.why: Correct: she meets the favourable predictors (low dose, > 2 years, tumour shrinkage) of both consensus statements.

options.text: Invasive macroprolactinoma with residual tumour and prolactin at the upper limit
options.why: Invasion and residual tumour lower the chance of remission.

options.text: Any patient after 6 months of normal prolactin
options.why: The consensus statements require at least 2 years and other criteria, not just normal prolactin.

items.explanation: In selected patients like case b, the Pituitary Society cites sustained remission in about 55% of microprolactinomas; afterwards, prolactin every 3 months in the first year and then annually.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman (fictional case) with schizophrenia stable on risperidone has amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea and a prolactin 4 times the upper limit; she has no headache or visual symptoms. What does the 2023 Pituitary Society consensus indicate?

options.text: Stop the risperidone yourself and repeat prolactin in 48 hours
options.why: Management requires collaboration with psychiatry (strong): it is not a unilateral gynaecology decision.
Starting an agonist requires caution and psychiatric input (weak).

options.text: Coordinate with psychiatry a dose reduction or a switch to a prolactin-sparing antipsychotic such as aripiprazole
options.why: Correct: it distinguishes the drug cause in most patients (strong) and requires collaboration with psychiatry.
There is no demonstrated lesion and no MRI criteria (> 10 times the limit, mass symptoms or other pituitary deficits).

items.explanation: Below 10 times the limit and without mass symptoms, antipsychotic-induced hyperprolactinaemia is expected; MRI is reserved for > 10 times the limit, mass symptoms or other pituitary deficits.

items.title: Before trying to conceive with a prolactinoma
items.core: The 2023 Pituitary Society consensus asks clinicians to inform people planning pregnancy of medical and surgical options (strong), suggests a baseline assessment shortly before (prolactin, visual fields and adenoma size) (weak) and, in macroprolactinoma, confirming agonist response before conception and considering surgery if there is none (strong). [[ref:petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus]] The 2025 Chinese consensus suggests shrinking a macroadenoma to microadenoma size before trying to conceive, and considers it unnecessary to stop the agonist in microprolactinoma while trying (very low; weak). [[ref:cpasc-2026-prolactinoma-consensus]]
items.body:
The Pituitary Society advises barrier rather than hormonal contraception to confirm treatment efficacy and learn the menstrual interval before pregnancy (weak), and informing patients of the risk of hypopituitarism if surgery is done first (strong). [[ref:petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus]] If hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism persists with normal prolactin and a wish for pregnancy, gonadotrophins are needed (strong). [[ref:petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus]] NICE NG257 offers cabergoline for ovulatory disorders due to hyperprolactinaemia. [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]

The Chinese consensus reports that prior treatment lowers the risk of macroadenoma growth in pregnancy from 18% to 4.7%, versus 1–5% in microadenomas. [[ref:cpasc-2026-prolactinoma-consensus]] In recurrent pregnancy loss with hyperprolactinaemia, ESHRE 2022 considers the evidence (a single small trial) insufficient to recommend bromocriptine. [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]
items.recall: What must be confirmed before a woman with macroprolactinoma tries to conceive, and which contraception is advised meanwhile?
items.pearl: With a macroadenoma, shrink it first with the agonist (or surgery if it does not respond), then pregnancy.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: Pituitary Society 2023, “Pregnancy and fertility” (p. 734), strong/weak per bullet; gonadotrophins under “Hypogonadism” (p. 728), strong. 2025 Chinese consensus, recommendation 31 (very low; weak). NICE NG257 1.32.1 [2026] (p. 38). ESHRE RPL 2022, section 14.5 (p. 119), no recommendation. In the 2023 Pituitary Society consensus, “strong” rests on moderate- or high-quality evidence and “weak” on low- or very-low-quality evidence (Box 1, p. 724). In the 2025 Chinese consensus, GRADE certainty runs from very low to high and strength is strong or weak; GPS = good practice statement.

items.title: Pregnancy: stop the agonist and monitor clinically
items.core: The 2023 Pituitary Society consensus recommends stopping the agonist as soon as pregnancy is confirmed (strong); in large macroprolactinomas, continuing it is also an option (strong). [[ref:petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus]] Microprolactinoma pregnancies are usually uneventful and are followed clinically every 3 months; macroprolactinomas monthly, with visual fields every 3 months, and MRI without gadolinium if growth is suspected (all strong). [[ref:petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus]]
items.body:
The consensus statements disagree on prolactin: the Pituitary Society recommends not using it to monitor growth during pregnancy (strong); the Chinese consensus does not recommend it in microadenomas, but in macroadenomas suggests measuring it every 2–3 months and reading a rise > 50% as possible growth together with the clinical picture (very low; weak). [[ref:petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus]] [[ref:cpasc-2026-prolactinoma-consensus]] Both propose restarting the agonist with clinically relevant growth and considering surgery if it does not respond; the Pituitary Society adds delivery if the pregnancy is sufficiently advanced. [[ref:petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus]] [[ref:cpasc-2026-prolactinoma-consensus]]

Most of the Pituitary Society panel prefers cabergoline at the lowest effective dose rather than switching to bromocriptine when trying to conceive (weak). [[ref:petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus]] The Chinese consensus reports a malformation rate of 3.9% with first-trimester bromocriptine, similar to the 2–4% background, and 2.7% with cabergoline, with no specific pattern. [[ref:cpasc-2026-prolactinoma-consensus]]
items.recall: What happens to the agonist once pregnancy is confirmed, how is a macroprolactinoma monitored, and where do the consensus statements disagree on prolactin?
items.pearl: Prolactin rises physiologically in pregnancy: watch headache and vision. According to the Chinese consensus, the number only helps in macroadenomas, and always together with clinical findings.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: Pituitary Society 2023, “Pregnancy and fertility” (pp. 734–735), strong except the cabergoline preference (weak). 2025 Chinese consensus, recommendations 32–35 (very low; weak). In the 2023 Pituitary Society consensus, “strong” rests on moderate- or high-quality evidence and “weak” on low- or very-low-quality evidence (Box 1, p. 724). In the 2025 Chinese consensus, GRADE certainty runs from very low to high and strength is strong or weak; GPS = good practice statement.

items.title: Breastfeeding with a prolactinoma
items.core: For the 2023 Pituitary Society consensus, breastfeeding is usually not contraindicated and may be allowed for a period, depending on whether treatment must be restarted to control the mass (strong). [[ref:petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus]] The 2025 Chinese consensus encourages breastfeeding and, if the situation requires an agonist, advises stopping it (very low; weak). [[ref:cpasc-2026-prolactinoma-consensus]]
items.body:
The Chinese consensus cites tumour growth during 12 months of breastfeeding of 1.2% in microadenomas and 4.3% in macroadenomas, and that 85–90% of micro- and 60–70% of macroadenomas need no agonist restart during lactation; it does not recommend breastfeeding while on the agonist. [[ref:cpasc-2026-prolactinoma-consensus]]

The Pituitary Society adds that the chance of resolution rises after a pregnancy, so these patients may try withdrawal of treatment (weak). [[ref:petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus]]
items.recall: Can a woman with a prolactinoma breastfeed, and what happens if she needs to restart the agonist?
items.pearl: The key question is not lactation prolactin but whether the tumour forces the agonist to be restarted.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: Pituitary Society 2023, “Pregnancy and fertility” (p. 735), strong; withdrawal after pregnancy under “Dopamine agonists: treatment withdrawal” (p. 731), weak. 2025 Chinese consensus, recommendation 36 (very low; weak). In the 2023 Pituitary Society consensus, “strong” rests on moderate- or high-quality evidence and “weak” on low- or very-low-quality evidence (Box 1, p. 724). In the 2025 Chinese consensus, GRADE certainty runs from very low to high and strength is strong or weak; GPS = good practice statement.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman (fictional case) with a microprolactinoma controlled on cabergoline has a positive pregnancy test. What is most appropriate per the 2023 Pituitary Society consensus?

options.text: Continue cabergoline until the end of the first trimester
options.why: Stopping it as soon as pregnancy is confirmed is recommended to reduce fetal exposure (strong).
Most of the panel does not routinely switch to bromocriptine; in a controlled microadenoma the indication is to stop.

options.text: Stop cabergoline and follow clinically every 3 months, without measuring prolactin
options.why: Correct: stop on confirmation and quarterly clinical follow-up (strong); prolactin is not useful to monitor growth.
MRI is reserved for suspected growth and is done without gadolinium.

items.explanation: The Chinese consensus agrees on stopping once pregnancy is confirmed in microadenoma (very low; weak), with a 1–5% risk of symptomatic growth.

items.stem: A woman 24 weeks pregnant (fictional case) with a macroprolactinoma, whose cabergoline was stopped when pregnancy was confirmed, reports severe headache and temporal visual field loss. What is indicated?

options.text: Measure prolactin and act on the value
options.why: The Pituitary Society recommends not using prolactin to assess growth in pregnancy (strong).

options.text: MRI without gadolinium and restart the agonist; surgery if there is no response
options.why: Correct: both consensus statements agree; if there is no response, surgery (the Pituitary Society adds delivery if the pregnancy is sufficiently advanced).
Growth with visual involvement requires immediate investigation and treatment.
The indicated test is MRI without gadolinium.

items.explanation: The Chinese consensus adds that 70–80% improve within 2–4 weeks of restarting the agonist and that, if surgery is needed, it is safer in the second trimester.

items.title: Case: Abril, long cycles and galactorrhoea

steps.text: Abril (fictional case), 31, has been trying to conceive with her partner, Bruno, for 10 months. Her cycles last 45–60 days and she has bilateral galactorrhoea. With an ovulatory disorder and galactorrhoea, NICE NG257 does indicate measuring prolactin, and so does the Pituitary Society. [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]] [[ref:petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus]]

Prolactin is 2.5 times the upper limit. First: negative pregnancy test, normal TSH, no antiemetics or psychotropics; because it is < 5 times the limit, it is repeated at rest and is raised again. [[ref:petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus]] [[ref:cpasc-2026-prolactinoma-consensus]]

With confirmed hyperprolactinaemia and no other cause, MRI shows a 6 mm microadenoma. Abril wants to conceive: the medical and surgical options are explained and she chooses cabergoline, the option of NICE and the Pituitary Society, with barrier contraception until her menstrual interval is known. [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]] [[ref:petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus]]

After 4 months her cycles are 30 days, with no galactorrhoea, and she stops barrier contraception. Two cycles later the pregnancy test is positive: she stops cabergoline and has clinical follow-up every 3 months, without prolactin measurement. After delivery she can breastfeed and, later, reassess whether she still needs the agonist. [[ref:petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus]] [[ref:cpasc-2026-prolactinoma-consensus]]

asrm-2021-fertility-evaluation.title: Fertility evaluation of infertile women: a committee opinion
asrm-2021-fertility-evaluation.authors: Practice Committee of the American Society for Reproductive Medicine
asrm-2021-fertility-evaluation.population: Women evaluated for infertility (including single women, same-sex couples, transgender men and non-binary patients seeking treatment); Fertil Steril 2021;116:1255–65.
asrm-2021-fertility-evaluation.finding: Evaluation at 12 months if <35 and at 6 months if ≥35; more immediate if >40; without delay with a known condition causing infertility. Evaluate both partners at the same time, with at least one semen analysis at onset. Basic work-up: ovulation, structure and patency of the reproductive tract, and semen analysis. With regular 21–35-day cycles, ovulation confirmation is not required (unless hirsutism). Female age is the single most important predictor of fecundity. Laparoscopy, postcoital test, thrombophilia, immunological tests, karyotype, endometrial biopsy, advanced sperm function testing and prolactin are not routine. Menstrual history may suffice to establish an ovulatory pattern; oligo/amenorrhoea establishes anovulation without further ovulation testing. If history is indeterminate: luteal progesterone (≈1 week before expected menses, not a fixed day such as day 21; >3 ng/mL = presumptive evidence of recent ovulation; a single value confirms ovulation, not luteal quality), urinary LH kits (false positives in PCOS) or transvaginal ultrasound. Basal body temperature and endometrial biopsy are not routinely recommended. Prolactin not routine; indicated with galactorrhoea or oligo/amenorrhoea.
asrm-2021-fertility-evaluation.limitations: Full text read (ASRM PDF). Committee opinion, not a GRADE guideline; US context; no formal strength or certainty grading.

cpasc-2026-prolactinoma-consensus.title: Chinese consensus on the diagnosis and treatment of prolactinomas (2025 edition)
cpasc-2026-prolactinoma-consensus.authors: Lin S, Chen Z, Ji L, Wang L, Zhang W, Tang X, Wu Y, Fan Q, Li J, Pan L, Yao Z, Deng C, Ye H, Li S, Zhu H, Zhao Y, Wang Y, Wu ZB; China Pituitary Adenoma Specialist Council
cpasc-2026-prolactinoma-consensus.population: Patients with prolactinoma (diagnosis, medical, surgical and radiation treatment, pregnancy and lactation). Panel of 60 experts from neurosurgery, endocrinology, obstetrics and gynaecology, neuroradiology, radiation oncology and methodology, supported by the MAGIC China Center (GRADE).
cpasc-2026-prolactinoma-consensus.finding: Measure prolactin with menstrual disorders, infertility or galactorrhoea in women of reproductive age (low certainty; strong); sample at rest, fasting and after at least 2 h awake; repeat if < 100 ng/ml. Macroprolactin when clinical findings are discordant (low; weak); dilution to exclude the hook effect in macroadenomas (low; weak). MRI after excluding other causes (low; weak). Asymptomatic microadenoma: observe (very low; weak). Periodic echocardiography with long-term high-dose cabergoline (low; weak). Withdrawal after > 2 years on a low maintenance dose with normal prolactin and tumour shrinkage (very low; weak). Microadenoma: no need to stop the agonist while trying to conceive, but stop it once pregnancy is confirmed (very low; weak). Breastfeeding: encouraged; if the agonist is needed, stop breastfeeding (very low; weak).
cpasc-2026-prolactinoma-consensus.limitations: Full text read (Chin Neurosurg J 2026;12:17, Europe PMC version, no page numbers). Chinese national consensus led by neurosurgery; most recommendations are weak with low or very low certainty. Cabergoline is unavailable in mainland China, so bromocriptine is its first choice, which shapes several recommendations. The supplementary tables could not be read.

eshre-2022-rpl.title: ESHRE guideline: recurrent pregnancy loss: an update in 2022
eshre-2022-rpl.authors: ESHRE Guideline Group on RPL; Bender Atik R, Christiansen OB, Elson J, et al.
eshre-2022-rpl.population: Couples with recurrent pregnancy loss (two or more losses).
eshre-2022-rpl.finding: Low-dose folic acid has not been shown to prevent loss in unexplained RPL (strong); do not use high doses without hyperhomocysteinaemia or conditions raising NTD risk (diabetes, epilepsy). Prophylactic vitamin D may be considered in preconception counselling (GPP) although evidence of effectiveness is absent; vitamin D testing to find a cause is not recommended. Multivitamins: advise options safe in pregnancy (GPP); they are not a treatment.
eshre-2022-rpl.limitations: Recommendations table and vitamin D chapter read in the full ESHRE PDF. Specific RPL population; several recommendations are good practice points (GPP), not trial-based.

eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.title: Evidence-based guideline: unexplained infertility
eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.authors: ESHRE Guideline Group on Unexplained Infertility; Romualdi D, et al.
eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.finding: With regular cycles, ovarian reserve testing is not required to identify the aetiology of infertility or to predict spontaneous conception over 6–12 months (strong recommendation, low certainty). IUI with ovarian stimulation first line (strong, very low certainty).
eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.limitations: Search up to October 2022; many recommendations with low or very low certainty. Full text read (journal summary via Europe PMC PMC10546081 and the full 114-page ESHRE guideline).

nice-2026-ng257.title: Fertility problems: assessment and treatment (NG257)
nice-2026-ng257.authors: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
nice-2026-ng257.population: People with fertility problems in the UK health system.
nice-2026-ng257.finding: Do not use AMH to predict clinical pregnancy through spontaneous conception (1.18.3). Use AMH or AFC as predictors of ovarian response to inform decisions and counselling about the likelihood of live birth after assisted conception (1.18.4). Do not use FSH as a predictor (1.18.5). Refer at presentation if the woman is 36 or over or there is a known cause or predisposing factors (1.16.8); otherwise investigation after 1 year of unprotected intercourse.
nice-2026-ng257.limitations: NHS (UK) context; replaces CG156. Numbering checked in the March 2026 PDF.

petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus.title: Diagnosis and management of prolactin-secreting pituitary adenomas: a Pituitary Society international Consensus Statement
petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus.authors: Petersenn S, Fleseriu M, Casanueva FF, Giustina A, Biermasz N, Biller BMK, Bronstein M, Chanson P, Fukuoka H, Gadelha M, Greenman Y, Gurnell M, Ho KKY, Honegger J, Ioachimescu AG, Kaiser UB, Karavitaki N, Katznelson L, Lodish M, Maiter D, Marcus HJ, McCormack A, Molitch M, Muir CA, Neggers S, Pereira AM, Pivonello R, Post K, Raverot G, Salvatori R, Samson SL, Shimon I, Spencer-Segal J, Vila G, Wass J, Melmed S
petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus.population: People with hyperprolactinaemia or prolactin-secreting pituitary adenomas (adults, pregnancy and fertility, children and adolescents, psychiatric disorders, menopause). International multidisciplinary Pituitary Society workshop with experts from 13 countries.
petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus.finding: Investigate prolactin with infertility, new menstrual irregularity, amenorrhoea or galactorrhoea (strong). With prolactin < 5 times the upper limit, repeat the measurement; use cannulated sampling if stress is suspected (strong). Review drugs, hypothyroidism, renal or liver failure and pregnancy (strong). Test macroprolactin when the rise is moderate (< 200 ng/ml), at least when clinical or imaging findings are discordant (strong); 1:100 dilution for a giant adenoma with normal or mildly raised prolactin (strong). MRI once hyperprolactinaemia is confirmed if no other cause is evident (strong). Cabergoline is the preferred agonist (strong). Echocardiography by dose (> 2.0 mg/week: baseline and every 2–3 years; ≤ 2.0 mg/week: after 5–6 years) (weak). Consider withdrawal with low doses, > 2 years of treatment and adenoma shrinkage (strong). Stop the agonist once pregnancy is confirmed (strong); do not use prolactin to monitor growth in pregnancy (strong); breastfeeding is usually not contraindicated (strong).
petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus.limitations: Full PDF read (Nat Rev Endocrinol 2023;19:722-740). Expert consensus by vote; grades “strong” (moderate or high evidence) and “weak” (low or very low) per Box 1 (p. 724), with no per-recommendation GRADE certainty. Literature up to January 2023. The supplementary boxes (including the pregnancy and withdrawal discussion) could not be read. Pituitary Society statement; not a fertility guideline.
